source: Hullermeier & Waegeman (2021) Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning
finding: The standard ML review on splitting uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic. It lists credal sets and credal inference as the set-valued alternative to a single Bayesian prior.
numbers: Review, no experiment. Credal inference (Sec 4.6) replaces one prior by a set of priors and returns a set of posteriors.
quote: Credal inference generalizes Bayesian inference by replacing a prior with a set of priors
limits: Credal methods are costly and rarely used on large models.
agent_relevance: Bridge from Keynes/Levi interval credences to ML: a wide set means 'we lack knowledge', not 'the world is random'.

source: Sale et al. (2024) Second-order uncertainty quantification: variance-based measures
finding: Proposes variance-based measures of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from second-order distributions. Notes that credal sets are the more general theory (Walley 1991).
numbers: Axiomatic analysis plus classification experiments; competitive with entropy-based measures.
limits: Classification only. Not tested on language models.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to read an 'unknown' flag: epistemic share of variance across sampled answers.

source: Sale et al. (2024) Label-wise aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty quantification
finding: Extends second-order uncertainty to per-class (label-wise) values, citing imprecise probabilities as background.
numbers: Per-class uncertainty measures; benchmark classification sets.
limits: Image and tabular classifiers, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Per-option uncertainty fits multi-hypothesis states in the schema.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Credal wrapper of model averaging for uncertainty estimation in classification
finding: Turns an ensemble of predictions into lower and upper probability per class (a credal set). Gives better out-of-distribution detection and lower calibration error on corrupted data than plain averaging.
numbers: Tested on CIFAR10/100, SVHN, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-O, with VGG16, ResNet, EfficientNet B2, ViT Base. Gains reported in AUROC/AUPRC tables.
limits: Vision classifiers, not language. Needs several ensemble members.
agent_relevance: Template: run N samples, report min and max per option, not the mean. Width of the interval flags 'unknown'.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty
finding: Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by meaning and measures spread. More predictive of accuracy than token-level baselines on QA.
numbers: Unsupervised; one model; QA datasets (AUROC values not extracted this session).
limits: Measures spread of answers, a single distribution, not an interval.
agent_relevance: Practical proxy for an interval: dispersion over meaning-classes of N samples.

source: Hou et al. (2024) Decomposing uncertainty for LLMs through input clarification ensembling
finding: Splits LLM uncertainty into input ambiguity (aleatoric) and model ignorance (epistemic) by rewriting the question into clarified versions and comparing answers.
numbers: Mistake detection on NQ and GSM8K, 200 validation items each; ambiguity detection on AmbigQA (200 items) and a self-built AmbigInst set. Total-uncertainty AUROC about the same as semantic entropy and deep ensembles. Ambiguity-detection AUROC for baseline ensembles on AmbigQA about 55 (text table partly garbled).
limits: Ambiguity labels are subtle and noisy. Gains depend on clarifier quality (Llama-3-8B fine-tuned vs GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Tells the agent whether a wide spread is fixable by asking (vague input) or by learning (missing knowledge).

source: Ling et al. (2024) Uncertainty quantification for in-context learning of LLMs
finding: Separates uncertainty from the demonstrations vs from the model, for in-context learning, using Llama-2 7B/13B/70B on classification sets.
numbers: AUPR and AUROC for misclassification detection across Emotion, Financial, AG_News and others; values mostly 0.4-0.8 (table garbled in text extraction, no single headline number read).
limits: Open Llama models only; classification.
agent_relevance: Choice of few-shot examples changes the epistemic part: scaffold design matters.

source: Kirchhof, Kasneci & Kasneci (2025) Position: uncertainty quantification needs reassessment for LLM agents
finding: Argues the aleatoric/epistemic split breaks down for interactive agents. Proposes three directions: underspecification uncertainty, interactive learning (ask follow-ups), and richer output uncertainty (more than one number).
numbers: Cites that GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k detects ambiguous questions with 57% accuracy (50% is chance) and humans rate only 53% of its follow-up questions as helpful.
quote: Popular definitions of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties directly contradict each other
limits: Position paper, no new experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports an 'unknown' flag tied to a clarifying question rather than a single probability. Matches the imprecise-credence aim.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? Confidence elicitation
finding: Verbalized confidence from LLMs is overconfident. Better prompts and sampling reduce but do not remove the problem.
numbers: Five LLMs (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2), eight tasks. Vanilla verbalized ECE above 0.377 average for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna. GPT-4 average AUROC only 62.7%. About 22.2% AUROC gain GPT-3 to GPT-4. GSM8K AUROC 54.8% to 92.7% with 5 samples plus consistency. White-box gap narrow: 0.522 vs 0.605 AUROC.
limits: No method wins everywhere; hard on professional-knowledge tasks.
agent_relevance: A point confidence is weak; the sample spread (a range) is the better signal.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalized confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several answer options with probabilities helps more.
numbers: Cuts expected calibration error by a relative 50% or more on ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2 (SciQ, TriviaQA, TruthfulQA).
quote: reduce expected calibration error by over 50%
limits: RLHF models only; not intervals.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt: 'give top-k answers with probabilities' acts like a crude credal spread.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice in the right format. P(True) self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples. P(IK) is trainable but calibrates poorly on new tasks.
numbers: Models up to 52B; many tasks. Calibration improves with scale.
limits: Calibration lost out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluating over many samples is an 'unknown' flag; trained P(IK) is the closest thing to an ignorance flag.

source: Yona, Aharoni & Geva (2024) Can LLMs faithfully express intrinsic uncertainty in words?
finding: Models answer decisively even when their own sampling is split. Faithfulness score close to the 0.5 chance level for all tested models.
numbers: Gemini family, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on Natural Questions and PopQA. Vanilla about 0.52-0.57. Best prompt cells reach 0.63 (GPT-4) and 0.70 (Gemini Ultra). Judge-vs-human correlation 0.97.
limits: Judge is itself an LLM (Gemini Ultra).
agent_relevance: Hedged text is not tied to real uncertainty by default. The flag must be computed from samples, then imposed on the answer.

source: Quach et al. (2024) Conformal language modeling
finding: Builds a set of candidate answers by sampling until a calibrated rule says the set contains an acceptable answer, with a coverage guarantee. Set-valued output, the frequentist cousin of an imprecise credence.
numbers: Distribution-free coverage guarantee; tested on open-domain QA, summarization and radiology report tasks.
limits: Needs a calibration set and an acceptability checker.
agent_relevance: If the set is large, the agent should say 'unknown'. Set size is the imprecision.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Benchmarking LLMs via uncertainty quantification
finding: Uses conformal prediction set size as the uncertainty measure for 9 LLMs on 5 tasks. Higher accuracy does not mean lower uncertainty.
numbers: Findings: higher-accuracy models may show lower certainty; larger models may be more uncertain; instruction fine-tuning raises uncertainty.
limits: Multiple-choice only.
agent_relevance: Set size is a usable imprecision number but is not tied to accuracy rank.

source: Liu et al. (2023) We're afraid language models aren't modeling ambiguity
finding: Builds AmbiEnt, 1,645 linguist-annotated ambiguous sentences, and finds LMs struggle to list the plausible readings.
numbers: GPT-4's disambiguations judged correct 32% of the time by crowdworkers vs 90% for the dataset's own disambiguations.
limits: Ambiguity is linguistic, not Ellsberg-type probability ambiguity.
agent_relevance: Models do not hold several readings at once, so the schema must force a list of readings.

source: Tamkin et al. (2022) Task ambiguity in humans and language models
finding: AmbiBench: six ambiguously specified classification tasks. Scale (175B) plus human-feedback training lets models match or beat humans; either alone is not enough. Fine-tuning on a few ambiguous in-context examples greatly lifts non-RLHF models.
numbers: Six tasks; humans vs GPT-3 variants; 95% bootstrap CIs; humans near 100% on negation, models near 50% when only the output format is understood.
limits: Small tasks, older models.
agent_relevance: Showing ambiguous examples in the prompt teaches models to keep the competing readings.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: Runs GPT-3 through classic decision tasks (descriptions, bandits, causal tasks). Good on described gambles, no directed exploration, poor causal reasoning. No Ellsberg or ambiguity test found in the paper text.
numbers: Battery of canonical experiments; small perturbations to vignettes sent GPT-3 'vastly astray'.
quote: it fails miserably in causal reasoning task
limits: GPT-3 only; keyword search of the full text found no Ellsberg experiment.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity aversion is not covered by this classic study; a gap for us.

source: Chen et al. (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT
finding: GPT budget choices in risk, time, social and food domains are mostly consistent with utility maximization and score higher than humans, but are sensitive to wording.
numbers: Rationality measured by CCEI (1 = perfect GARP). GPT beat human participants in the parallel experiment. Cites Ahn et al. (2014) on ambiguity aversion but does not test it.
limits: No ambiguity condition.
agent_relevance: Consistency alone does not tell us whether the model treats unknown odds differently.

source: Ross, Kim & Lo (2024) LLM economicus?
finding: Fits utility curves to many LLMs: neither human-like nor rational, and inconsistent across settings. Prompting can shift the biases.
numbers: Open and closed models; risk-aversion, time-discount and framing probes with probability-based prospects.
limits: Risk (known odds) only; no ambiguity condition.
agent_relevance: Behavior shifts with prompt, so any ambiguity attitude must be set by the scaffold, not assumed.

source: Jia et al. (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs under uncertain context
finding: ChatGPT-4.0-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus and Gemini-1.0-pro show risk aversion, loss aversion and overweighting of small probabilities, with large differences between models.
numbers: Three commercial LLMs; multiple-choice-list task; context-free vs demographic personas. NeurIPS 2024.
limits: Risk, not ambiguity. Persona prompts change estimates.
agent_relevance: Prompt framing moves risk attitude; likely the same for ambiguity attitude.

source: Search note (2026-11-17) Direct LLM tests of the Ellsberg paradox or imprecise credences
finding: No paper found that tests LLMs on the Ellsberg urn or on Keynes/Levi imprecise credences. WebSearch budget was exhausted and arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429, so this is a search gap, not proof of absence.
numbers: Zero direct hits among the papers opened; Crossref returned no LLM-Ellsberg item.
limits: Must be rechecked later with working search.
agent_relevance: Open task: run an Ellsberg two-urn test on our model with and without an 'unknown' flag.

source: Walley (1991) Statistical reasoning with imprecise probabilities (cited in Sale 2024 and Wang 2024)
finding: Foundational book for lower/upper previsions. Seen only as a citation in opened ML papers, not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Background for the unknown flag; no direct use.

source: Cross-check of credal ML papers (Wang 2024; Sale 2024)
finding: Both credal ML papers stay with image and tabular classifiers; none found applied to token-level LLM output.
numbers: Compare c04, c02.
limits: Search was limited.
agent_relevance: Credal prediction on LLMs is an open niche.

source: Design note from Xiong 2024 and Tian 2023: interval from samples vs verbalized interval
finding: Across Xiong and Tian, sample-consistency beat verbalized confidence for failure prediction; verbalized numbers cluster high.
numbers: GSM8K AUROC 54.8% (verbalized) to 92.7% (5 samples, consistency); Tian relative ECE gain over 50%.
limits: Task-dependent.
agent_relevance: Build the unknown flag from N samples plus consistency, not from asking for an interval.

source: Kirchhof 2025 on clarifying questions as uncertainty reduction
finding: Under-specified user input turns apparent epistemic uncertainty into aleatoric uncertainty; asking follow-ups reduces it, but too many questions lose the user.
numbers: Models detect ambiguity at 57% vs 50% chance; humans find 53% of generated follow-ups helpful.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: The unknown flag should trigger one targeted question, not a refusal.

source: Hou 2024 limits on separating ambiguity from ignorance
finding: Authors note ambiguity in AmbigQA is 'sometimes subtle', so labels may undercount true ambiguity, capping measured detection quality.
numbers: AmbigQA aleatoric AUROC near 55 for ensemble baselines.
limits: Caveat from paper text.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a clean epistemic/aleatoric split; treat the flag as a heuristic.

source: Kadavath 2022 limit: P(IK) fails out of distribution
finding: Trained 'I know' predictor generalizes only partly across tasks and calibration is poor on new tasks.
numbers: Partial generalization; calibration poor on new tasks.
limits: Anthropic models of 2022.
agent_relevance: A trained ignorance flag must be re-checked per domain.
